edges.description: Mutagenic injury selects for loss of p53-mediated genomic surveillance.
Loss of checkpoint control enables continued tumor cell proliferation.
Proliferating malignant clones invade adjacent sinus walls and bone.
Advancing tumors establish an immune-evasive microenvironment that supports continued growth.
Inhaled wood dust deposits on and chronically injures the sinonasal epithelium; this is the route by which the mutagenic stress modeled by this node is established in occupationally exposed patients.
Chronic inhalation of nickel compounds delivers a genotoxic metal burden to the sinonasal epithelium, establishing the mutagenic epithelial injury modeled by this node.

evidence.reference_title: TP53 mutations and CDKN2A mutations/deletions are highly recurrent molecular alterations in the malignant progression of sinonasal papillomas
evidence.snippet: highly recurrent TP53 mutations, CDKN2A mutations, and/or CDKN2A copy-number losses were detected; overall, nearly all tumors (n = 28/29; 96.6%) harbored at least one TP53 or CDKN2A alteration.

evidence.snippet: Although immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have shown efficacy in head and neck cancers (HNCs), clinical data specific to SNSCC are scarce.

nodes.description: Because the paranasal sinuses are bounded by thin bony walls adjacent to the orbit and skull base, progressive tumor growth invades local tissues, erodes bone, and can extend into the orbit and intracranial compartment, accounting for the high rate of advanced presentation and the need for open craniofacial surgery in a large proportion of cases.

evidence.reference_title: Sinonasal Squamous Cell Carcinoma, a Narrative Reappraisal of the Current Evidence
evidence.snippet: Surgery represents the pivot of treatment and is performed through an endoscopic transnasal approach whenever feasible. Open surgery is required for a large proportion of cases.

nodes.description: Inhaled nickel compounds in refining, smelting, plating, cutlery and alkaline battery manufacture are an established cause of sinonasal cancer. Unlike wood dust, which is preferentially associated with adenocarcinoma, the nickel-associated tumors reported from refinery cohorts are predominantly squamous, making this the occupational exposure most specifically tied to the squamous subtype.

evidence.snippet: In the most nickel-exposed work site (refinery), there were 14 lung cancers (SIR 2.01) and 3 sinonasal cancers (SIR 26.7, 95%).

nodes.description: Occupational inhalation of wood dust is an established cause of sinonasal cancer, with prolonged exposure linked to malignant transformation of the sinonasal epithelium. The pooled association is far stronger for sinonasal adenocarcinoma than for squamous cell carcinoma, so wood dust is better read as a shared sinonasal carcinogen with a histology-dependent effect size than as the dominant driver of the squamous subtype.
